title: You Don’t Actually Want Them Dead. You Just Keep Imagining a Life Where They Finally Hurt Like You Did.
paragraphs: You Don’t Actually Want Them Dead. You Just Keep Imagining a Life Where They Finally Hurt Like You Did.
The revenge you would never admit out loud may not look like murder. Sometimes it looks like imagining the day they finally realize what they did to you—and secretly hoping that realization hurts.
You would never say you want them dead.
That sounds too cruel.
Too dark.
Too unlike you.
You don't lie awake plotting how to destroy them. You aren't looking for ways to ruin their life. You probably wouldn't even describe yourself as vengeful.
You just imagine things sometimes.
You imagine their new relationship collapsing.
You imagine the person who replaced you eventually seeing what you saw.
You imagine their friends discovering who they really are.
You imagine the career they chose over you suddenly falling apart.
You imagine them scrolling through your life years from now and realizing they lost someone who genuinely loved them.
You imagine them hearing that you're finally happy without them.
You imagine the apology.
The trembling voice.
The regret.
The moment they finally understand how badly they wounded you.
And somewhere inside that imaginary scene is a sentence you may never actually say:
“Now you know how it feels.”
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because sometimes resentment doesn't scream.
Sometimes it daydreams.
Sometimes revenge never reaches our hands because it has already built a theater inside our minds.
And Jesus walks straight into that theater.
Not to humiliate the wounded.
Not to pretend the betrayal didn't matter.
Not to command abused people to remain accessible to unsafe people.
Not to call evil good.
He comes to rescue the wounded heart from becoming spiritually chained to the person who wounded it.
Jesus said:

“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου καὶ μισήσεις τὸν ἐχθρόν σου. ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν· ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς, ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς…”
Matthew 5:43–45.
In straightforward English:

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven…”
Listen carefully to the language Jesus uses.
“ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν.”
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn.
“Love your enemies.”

The verb ἀγαπᾶτε, agapate, comes from ἀγαπάω, agapaō. Jesus is not commanding His disciples to manufacture warm sentimental feelings toward people who harmed them. Biblical love is deeper and more demanding than emotional affection. It seeks what accords with God's good rather than surrendering itself to hatred.
Then Jesus makes the command painfully concrete:
“καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς.”
“And pray for those who persecute you.”
Pray.
For them.
And suddenly Christianity stops being theoretical.
Because it is easy to post about forgiveness when nobody has betrayed you.
It is easy to quote grace when nobody has humiliated you.
It is easy to talk about loving enemies when your enemy doesn't have a name, a face, a phone number, and a place in your memories.
But yours might.
Maybe it was your father.
Your mother.
Your former spouse.
The person who cheated.
The friend who betrayed your confidence.
The pastor who disappointed you.
The relative who lied about you.
The coworker who sabotaged you.
The person who abandoned you precisely when you needed them most.
Maybe they never apologized.
Maybe they apologized badly.
Maybe everyone believed their version.
Maybe they walked away looking innocent while you were left carrying consequences they helped create.
And that is why your imagination became the courtroom you never received in real life.
Inside your head, you finally get justice.
They lose.
You win.
They cry.
You watch.
They regret leaving.
You don't take them back.
They finally understand your value.
They finally feel the loneliness you felt.
And for several imaginary seconds, something inside you feels satisfied.
Then the scene disappears.
But the resentment remains.
Here is the question that may expose what anger has been hiding:
If God completely restored the person who hurt you—without first letting you watch them suffer—would you be disappointed?
Don't answer quickly.

If they genuinely repented tomorrow, found mercy in Christ, rebuilt their life, became emotionally healthy, experienced a beautiful marriage, received opportunities, laughed again, slept peacefully, and spent eternity forgiven by the same Jesus who forgave you…
would some part of you whisper:
“That isn't fair”?
There it is.
That place.
That little locked room inside the heart.
Jesus wants that room too.
Because the Gospel is scandalous precisely here.
We love grace when it comes looking for us.
Grace becomes harder to celebrate when it starts knocking on our enemy's door.
We sing about the blood of Jesus washing away our sins, then quietly wonder whether the blood should wash theirs quite so thoroughly.
We want the cross to be sufficient for us.
But sometimes we want consequences to have the final word over them.
Then we remember who was hanging on that cross.
Jesus Christ.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Stripped.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
And while experiencing an injustice infinitely greater than the petty offenses we sometimes obsess over, He prayed:
“Father, forgive them…”
Luke 23:34.
That does not make evil insignificant.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
Christian forgiveness does not mean saying, “What happened didn't matter.”
It mattered.
The betrayal mattered.
The manipulation mattered.
The lies mattered.
The abandonment mattered.
The nights you cried mattered.
The trust that was shattered mattered.
Forgiveness is not amnesia.
It is not necessarily reconciliation.
It is not automatically restored trust.
It is not removing wise boundaries.
It is not refusing lawful justice.
It is not remaining in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Scripture never requires you to pretend darkness is light.
Forgiveness means something more radical:
You surrender ultimate vengeance to God.
Paul writes:
Romans 12:19.
Why?
Because immediately before that, Scripture says:
“Repay no one evil for evil…”
Romans 12:17.
And shortly afterward:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
Romans 12:21.
Do you see the danger?
The person who hurt you already took something.
Don't let resentment take more.
Don't let them take your peace after they already took your trust.
Don't let them occupy your imagination after they already occupied enough of your history.
Don't let their sin disciple your heart.
Don't let what they did determine who you become.
There is a kind of captivity where the prison door is open but you keep returning to the cell because your enemy is still sitting there in your imagination.
You replay the conversation.
Rewrite your response.
Imagine their downfall.
Check whether life has humbled them yet.
Wonder whether their relationship is failing.
Wonder whether they miss you.
Wonder whether karma finally found their address.
And every time you return, the wound gets another vote in your identity.
Jesus offers something better than revenge.
Freedom.
But freedom sometimes begins with a prayer you don't feel ready to pray.
“Jesus, I don't know how to love them yet.
But I don't want hatred to own me anymore.
I confess that part of me has wanted them to hurt.
I have imagined their humiliation.
I have secretly wanted proof that losing me destroyed something in them.
Forgive me.
Heal what they wounded.
Judge what needs judgment.
Correct what needs correction.
Protect whoever needs protection.
Bring truth into whatever remains hidden.
And if they can be brought to repentance, bring them to repentance.
Save them.
Change them.
Have mercy on them.
And please, Jesus…
have mercy on me too.”
That prayer may hurt.
Pray it anyway.
Not because the offender deserves control over your emotions.
Because Jesus deserves control over your heart.
You are not forgiving because sin was small.
You forgive because Christ is greater.
You are not surrendering vengeance because justice doesn't matter.
You surrender it because God is a better Judge than you are.
You are not praying for your enemy because you're weak.
You are praying because Jesus refuses to let hatred reproduce itself inside His disciples.
Remember Stephen.
Acts 7 records a man being murdered while faithfully bearing witness to Christ.
Stones struck his body.
His enemies surrounded him.
And near death, Stephen cried:
“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
Acts 7:60.
Where does a human being find that kind of mercy?
Not in personality.
Not in motivational slogans.
Not in pretending pain doesn't hurt.
Stephen had seen the glory of God.
He belonged to Jesus.
That changes what a person can release.
And perhaps this is where your story changes too.
Not when they apologize.
Not when they finally understand.
Not when everybody learns the truth.
Not when their life collapses.
Not when you receive the closure you thought you needed.
Maybe freedom begins tonight when you finally confess:
“Jesus, I've been secretly rehearsing revenge.”
There is no reason to hide that from Him.
He already knows.
And still He calls you closer.
The Gospel doesn't merely forgive the sins everyone knows about.
Jesus goes after the hidden ones too.
The respectable bitterness.
The silent jealousy.
The imaginary arguments.
The private courtroom.
The fantasy of their downfall.
The satisfaction you feel when you hear they're struggling.
The hope that someday they'll look at your happiness and hate themselves for losing you.
Bring that too.
Bring the ugly part.
Bring the sentence you would never put beneath your Christian profile picture.
Bring the resentment you carefully renamed “discernment.”
Bring the revenge you renamed “wanting them to learn their lesson.”
Bring it to Christ.
Because repentance is not God crushing a wounded person.
Repentance is turning away from sin and returning to the One who can actually heal the wound beneath it.
Maybe underneath your anger is grief.
Maybe underneath your revenge fantasy is a desperate question:
“Did what they did to me matter?”
Yes.
It mattered.
But their suffering cannot heal yours.
Their loneliness cannot restore what you lost.
Their regret cannot become your resurrection.
Their downfall cannot give you a new heart.
Only Jesus can reach that deeply.
This is why Christ doesn't merely command forgiveness and then abandon us to manufacture it ourselves.
The Christian life flows from grace received.
“We love because he first loved us.”
1 John 4:19.
Before you were the wounded person trying to forgive, you were a sinner needing forgiveness.
So was I.
That levels the ground beneath the cross.
Not because every sin has identical earthly consequences.
Not because victim and offender become morally interchangeable.
They do not.
But because every redeemed human being ultimately stands before God by mercy.
You don't enter heaven because you were better at being hurt than somebody else was at hurting you.
You enter through Christ.
Through His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His grace.
That is why the Gospel can do what revenge cannot.
Revenge says, “I will finally have peace when they hurt.”
Jesus says, in effect, “Give Me the wound, and I will begin making you free whether they ever understand it or not.”
Imagine that freedom.
Imagine hearing their name without your stomach tightening.
Imagine seeing them succeed without feeling personally insulted.
Imagine no longer checking whether consequences caught up with them.
Imagine praying sincerely that God would bring them to repentance rather than secretly hoping life destroys them.
Imagine waking up and realizing you haven't rehearsed that old conversation in weeks.
Imagine discovering that their memory no longer controls the temperature of your soul.
That is not losing.
That is healing.
That is grace defeating what happened to you without denying what happened to you.
And perhaps someday the person who wounded you really will collapse.
Perhaps consequences will come.
Perhaps truth will surface.
Perhaps they will finally understand.
But if that day comes, may your heart have been so transformed by Jesus that instead of whispering, “Good,” something inside you whispers:
“Lord, have mercy.”
Because that is what somebody once prayed over sinners like us.
There is another reason Jesus gives in Matthew 5 that we cannot ignore.

He tells His disciples to love their enemies and pray for their persecutors “so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven,” then points to God's common kindness: He causes His sun to rise on evil and good and sends rain on the righteous and unrighteous.
The Father's generosity exposes our instinct to reserve kindness only for people we believe have earned it.
Christ calls His people into a family resemblance.
Not sentimental passivity.
Holy love.
Truth without hatred.
Boundaries without revenge.
Justice without personal vengeance.
Discernment without dehumanization.
And prayer even when the name in that prayer still hurts.
Maybe you need to stop reading for a moment and say their name before God.
Not publicly.
Not dramatically.
Just you and Jesus.
Say it.
Then pray:

“Lord Jesus Christ, I surrender my right to personally avenge myself. I will not call evil good. I will not pretend the wound never happened. Give me wisdom for boundaries, courage for truth, and grace to forgive. I place this person into Your hands. Bring repentance where repentance is needed. Bring justice where justice is needed. Protect those who need protection. Heal what has been damaged in me. Forgive my secret hatred, my imagined revenge, and every moment I have enjoyed the thought of their pain. Teach me to love as someone who has been loved by You. Amen.”
And tomorrow, you may have to pray it again.
Forgiveness can be a decisive act of obedience while emotional healing unfolds over time.
Memories may return.
Anger may return.
The imaginary courtroom may reopen.
When it does, take the case back out of your hands.
Give it to God again.
Seventy times seven if necessary.
Not as arithmetic for tolerating abuse, but as the refusal to turn forgiveness into a tiny quota, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 18:21–22.
You don't need their destruction to prove your pain was real.
You don't need their regret to prove you were valuable.
You don't need them crawling back to prove you were worth loving.
Calvary already says something infinitely greater about where your worth and hope are found:
Jesus Christ gave Himself to redeem sinners.
And if you belong to Him, the person who wounded you does not get to write your ending.
Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
From betrayal…
to healing.
From resentment…
to surrender.
From private revenge fantasies…
to hands finally opened before God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be truthful.
Or simply tell your testimony. Someone reading quietly may discover that they are not the only believer who has had to drag bitterness into the light and surrender it to Jesus.
Send it privately to the friend whose heart has been exhausted by betrayal.
Share it with the Christian who knows Scripture but is struggling to live it.
Share it with the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely about behaving nicely and needs to see that Jesus goes after the deepest chambers of the human heart.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront hidden sin, heal through truth, and keep Jesus Christ at the center, follow and stay connected.

Sharing these articles is another. Neither purchases the favor of God, and neither earns salvation—salvation is God's gift in Christ, received by grace through faith. But Christians are called to use what God has entrusted to them to serve, encourage, teach, give, and help the Gospel go farther. If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, you can help place these messages before people who may never walk into a church but might stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
Think about Jesus.
The Jesus who saw every wound.
The Jesus who knows every hidden thought.
The Jesus who refuses to flatter our resentment.
The Jesus who commands us to love our enemies.
The Jesus who carried sin to the cross.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who forgives repentant sinners.
The Jesus who can heal wounded hearts without requiring the destruction of the people who wounded them.
And the Jesus who can look at the darkest room inside you—the room where you've replayed their downfall a thousand times—and say:
“Give Me this room too.”
Maybe that is the real miracle you have been waiting for.
Not watching them finally hurt like you did.
But waking up one day and realizing you no longer need them to.
Because the greatest evidence that Jesus has healed your wound may not be that you finally forgot what they did.
It may be that you remember—and no longer need their suffering to make your heart feel whole.
